source: Electricity flows only around a complete loop called a closed circuit: from the battery, through the wires and the bulb, and back. A switch opens the loop to turn the bulb off.
Thinking one wire from the battery to the bulb is enough. The current needs a path out of the battery and a path back in.
A flashlight has a battery, a bulb, a switch and metal strips joining them. Together they make a circuit.

Electricity flows only around a complete loop, a closed circuit: out of one end of the battery, through the wires and the bulb, and back into the other end. If the loop has a gap, it is an open circuit and the bulb stays dark.
Tap the switch to open and close the circuit.
A switch is a little bridge in the loop. Turned on, it closes the gap. Turned off, it opens the gap and the current stops.
The battery pushes electric charges around the loop like a pump pushing water around a ring of pipes. A break anywhere stops the whole flow.
A wire goes from the top of a battery to a bulb, but no wire goes from the bulb back to the battery. Does the bulb light?
The current needs a path out and a path back.
There is no path back, so the loop is open.
Thinking one wire is enough because "the electricity goes to the bulb". It must go through the bulb and back.
